newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook-Factors conspire to limit market.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook-Factors conspire to limit market.

text.p: A combination of the over-the-counter (OTC) options expiry on Tuesday, the long Easter weekend and month-end book squaring should limit gold prices to a cautious range this week, dealer said.
"If the market wasn't so quiet anyway, this could be quite interesting," one dealer said.
"As it is, the gold price is likely to remain whippy but in a pretty narrow range," the dealer added.
Apart from a break-out to test support which held at $346 per ounce, gold was limited within a $350.00-$355.00 range all of last week.
What happens next has brought mixed opinions from the market professionals.
One analyst based in continental Europe argued that that last year's pattern of gold prices falling after the options expired was not so consistent this year.
"When prices were falling there was a tendency for put option grantors to sell their hedges after the expiry," he explained, which would exacerbate a downward move.
"Now with grantors offering calls, there may still be some naked calls around after the expiry which they will need to cover," he added, saying this would help the price to rise.
An option gives its holder the right but not the obligation to buy or sell a commodity at a set price known as the strike price.
A call option is the right to buy and a put the right to sell.
Other market players favoured prices drifting off after the expiry but with the downside limited to around $350.00.
Technically gold has ample support backed by proven physical buying at the lower levels, according to dealers and analysts.

However this has yet to translate into a rally and comments from U.S. Federal Reserve Bank chairman Alan Greenspan last week which hinted strongly at an interest rate rise did not promote confidence in gold.

Referring to the Comex April contract, Elli Gifford at Investment Research of Cambridge said, "There are signs that the selling pressure is slackening off now, adding to the likelihood that the supports reaching down to the recent lows will hold."
However, Gifford added that there were no signs of a sustainable recovery in place yet.
A 0.25 percent rise has been assumed and unless it was radically higher little reaction was likely, analysts said.
